items.x_text:
BTCPay Server: attackers are draining Bitcoin and Litecoin from hot wallets on outdated instances (2.4.1 or older). BTCPay says upgrade to 2.4.7, and if you were on an old version, move to a fresh server with a new wallet.

#CryptoSecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Your payment server was outdated. Your hot wallet is now empty. 💸

What BTCPay Server warned (via The Hacker News, 3 Nov):
→ Attackers drained Bitcoin and Litecoin from hot wallets on outdated BTCPay Server instances
→ The targeted servers ran 2.4.1 (July 2026) or earlier
→ Reports began surfacing around 1 Nov; BTCPay shared two wallet addresses linked to the thefts
→ The method differs from the August flaw that exposed Lightning node credentials
→ Latest release 2.4.7 also fixes one critical and several medium bugs found by Anthropic's OSS scanner

What to do: upgrade to 2.4.7. If you ran 2.4.1 or older, move to a fresh server with a new wallet even if nothing looks stolen, treat every stored secret as compromised, and keep only daily operating funds in the hot wallet.

items.send_to: whoever patches your Linux web servers

cover.hook: Your security tool updated itself. The update was the attack.
cover.sub: cPGuard's update channel was hijacked. 2,946 servers affected, says the developer.

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: cPGuard is a Linux web-server security suite used with cPanel, DirectAdmin and Plesk. On 2 Nov at 02:06 UTC an attacker used stolen credentials to reach the update CDN and pushed a malicious script to versions 5.88.12 to 5.88.19.

slides.label: servers affected
slides.note: Per an OpsShield spokesperson to BleepingComputer; its billing database was also copied

slides.title: What it took
slides.body: The script went after Linux password hashes, root MySQL/MariaDB config, root shell history and root SSH files. OpsShield says 32 files were pulled from each customer, sent out via its own licensing server. Distribution stopped within 12 hours.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: Security agents run as root and auto-update. Whoever controls the update channel controls every server. Your most trusted tool is also your biggest blast radius.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Update every cPGuard server to 5.88.25 or later
Reset passwords, rotate DB creds, cloud secrets and SSH keys
Check root SSH authorized_keys on hosted servers
List which agents on your servers auto-update as root

items.question: Which tool on your servers can push code as root without anyone approving it?
items.x_text:
cPGuard (OpsShield): an attacker hijacked the Linux security suite's update channel and pushed a data-stealing script to 5.88.12–5.88.19. OpsShield: 2,946 servers affected. Update to 5.88.25+ and rotate SSH keys and DB credentials.

#SupplyChainAttack #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:

What happened (BleepingComputer, 3 Nov):
→ cPGuard is a Linux web-server security suite used alongside cPanel, DirectAdmin and Plesk
→ On 2 Nov at 02:06 UTC, an attacker used compromised credentials to reach OpsShield's update CDN and pushed a malicious script to versions 5.88.12 to 5.88.19
→ It targeted password hashes, root database config, root shell history and root SSH files
→ OpsShield says 2,946 servers were affected, 32 files were retrieved per customer, and its billing database was copied
→ Distribution was stopped within 12 hours

What to do: update to 5.88.25 or later, reset passwords, rotate database credentials, cloud secrets and SSH keys, and review root SSH access.

cover.hook: 1.3 million school staff and students. One flaw in someone else's software.
cover.sub: The Frontline Education breach is now counted at over 1.3 million people (SecurityWeek).

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: Frontline Education makes admin software for K-12 school districts. It says a vulnerability in a third-party product it uses allowed access to part of its environment holding Frontline Central and School Health Management data.

slides.label: people impacted
slides.note: School district staff and students, per SecurityWeek (3 Nov 2026)

slides.title: What was exposed
slides.body: Reports from districts name Social Security numbers, home addresses and email addresses. Frontline identified the flaw on 14 Aug; districts were still telling staff in October.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: One vendor holds data for many districts. SSNs plus home addresses fuel tax scams, new account fraud and convincing phishing aimed at teachers.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Tell staff to freeze credit at all three bureaus
Warn staff about tax and payroll phishing
Ask every ed-tech vendor which of your records they hold
Check if similar third-party access paths exist

items.question: Does your district know which vendors hold staff Social Security numbers?
items.x_text:
Frontline Education breach now impacts over 1.3 million school district staff and students, per SecurityWeek. A flaw in third-party software exposed data incl. SSNs and home addresses. Districts are advising credit freezes.

#DataBreach #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
1.3 million school staff and students. One flaw in someone else's software. 🏫

What we know:
→ SecurityWeek reports the Frontline Education breach impacts over 1.3 million people, school district staff and students
→ Frontline makes admin software for K-12 districts; it says a vulnerability in a third-party product allowed access to part of its environment
→ Data reported by districts: Social Security numbers, home addresses, email addresses
→ Frontline identified the flaw on 14 Aug; districts were still notifying staff in October
→ Frontline says it fixed the flaw, brought in an outside firm and notified law enforcement

What to do: freeze credit at all three bureaus if you were notified, expect tax and payroll phishing, and ask your ed-tech vendors exactly which records they hold.

#Ransomware #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
The patch is from 2024. The ransomware is from this week. 🗄️

What Synology warned (via The Hacker News, 3 Nov):
→ Attackers are exploiting a DSM vulnerability patched back in 2024 to target NAS devices on outdated versions
→ The goal: encrypt data and extort victims
→ Customers report C3RB3R ransomware, which renames files with a ".L0CK3D" extension
→ Synology didn't name the exact flaw; The Hacker News links it to advisory Synology_SA_24_20

What to do: update DSM on every Synology box today, enable automatic updates, keep the admin interface off the internet, and make sure backups live somewhere the NAS can't overwrite.
